Summary

This paper introduces a new task setting for product attribute mining: lightly supervised open-world attribute mining, where the system must both expand values for known seed attribute types and discover values for previously unseen attribute types without explicit type descriptions. To support this setting, the authors construct a new dataset, WoaM, spanning four Amazon product categories and including titles and bullet points. They propose Amacer, a pipeline with three main ingredients: syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, and two additional regularizers for unseen attribute discovery: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence objective and an unsupervised latent-attribute/topic-style objective. Final grouping combines adaptive expansion for seed types with DBSCAN for remaining candidates. Experiments show improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines, with especially strong gains in overall pseudo-F1 and on new attribute types.

Overall assessment

I think this is a meaningful and timely paper. The problem formulation is interesting and practically motivated: in real e-commerce settings, attribute inventories are incomplete and evolving, and requiring explicit descriptions of all new target attributes is unrealistic. The paper also contributes a dataset that appears more realistic than prior title-only settings by including bullet points and emphasizing unseen values/types. The method is sensible and reasonably well engineered for the weak-supervision regime. Empirically, the gains over prior open-world baselines are substantial.

That said, I also have several concerns. The evaluation protocol is somewhat unconventional and makes it hard to interpret the practical significance of the reported gains. The method is a pipeline with multiple heuristics, and some of the strongest gains may come from candidate generation rather than the proposed representation learning. The novelty of some components is moderate, since they combine known ingredients (contrastive learning, topic-model-like latent variables, DBSCAN, prototype-style expansion) in this application. Finally, the dataset scope is still limited to four categories and English Amazon text, so claims about general open-world attribute mining should be tempered.

Strengths

1. Clear practical motivation
The paper addresses a realistic gap between closed-world extraction and zero-shot extraction with explicit type names. The proposed setting is well motivated for e-commerce.

2. Useful dataset contribution
WoaM appears valuable: it includes both titles and bullet points, has a substantial proportion of unseen values and unseen types, and uses a curated seed set rather than purely noisy distant supervision.

3. Strong empirical gains
The reported improvements over OA-Mine and other baselines are large, especially in the main pseudo-F1 metric and on new-type discovery.

4. Thoughtful handling of weak supervision
The use of seed supervision plus implicit contextual signals is a reasonable design for this setting. The decomposition into seed expansion and new-type discovery is intuitive.

5. Good analysis
The paper includes decomposed results for seed vs new types and title vs bullet points, plus qualitative examples and discussion of failure modes.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. Evaluation metric is hard to justify
The main metric is a “pseudo-F1” built from averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as pseudo-precision and combining with recall. This is unusual and not standard. Jaccard/ARI/NMI are clustering agreement metrics with different properties; averaging them and treating the result as precision is not theoretically grounded. Because the paper’s main claims rely on this metric, the conclusions are harder to assess.

2. Candidate generation may dominate improvements
The syntax-based candidate generation appears to be a major source of gains over segmentation-based OA-Mine. This is not a problem in itself, but it means the contribution may be more about better candidate extraction than better open-world attribute discovery. The paper partially acknowledges this, but the framing still emphasizes the latent-attribute regularization. More controlled experiments are needed to isolate where the gains come from.

3. Limited novelty of modeling components
Most components are adaptations of existing ideas: supervised contrastive learning, skip-gram-like co-occurrence regularization, neural topic modeling, prototype/adaptive threshold expansion, and DBSCAN. The novelty lies more in the formulation and integration than in fundamentally new modeling ideas.

4. Limited dataset breadth
Only four categories are used, all from Amazon and in English. It is unclear how robust the approach is across more diverse categories, noisier domains, multilingual settings, or categories with very different attribute structures.

5. Dependence on POS tagging and profile-derived patterns
The candidate generation relies on POS tagging quality and on POS patterns extracted from product profiles. This may encode category/domain-specific biases and may not transfer well when profile resources are unavailable or noisier.

6. Weakness on actual span extraction remains substantial
Table 5 shows low exact span F1 and low precision. This suggests that while clustering/grouping may improve, the end-to-end extraction problem remains far from solved. The paper is honest about this, but the practical utility may be limited unless candidate quality improves further.

Detailed comments

Task formulation and dataset

The task formulation is one of the strongest parts of the paper. It is a natural next step beyond closed-world and zero-shot settings. I especially appreciate that the outputs are evaluated as clusters rather than requiring names for unseen types.

The dataset construction seems careful, especially the hybrid seed-set curation. However, I would like more detail on annotation quality:
- What is inter-annotator agreement on span boundaries and type assignments?
- How were disagreements resolved?
- Since “reasonable attribute values” is subjective, some measure of consistency is important.
- How many test products per category are annotated?

The paper says no overlapping spans are allowed and each span gets a single type. This simplifies evaluation, but may suppress realistic cases where a phrase could express multiple attributes or nested values. A brief discussion of how often this matters would help.

Method

The syntax-based candidate generation is simple and practical. In fact, it may be one of the most useful contributions. Still, I would like more quantitative evidence on candidate quality:
- Candidate recall against gold spans
- Candidate precision or average candidates per product
- Comparison with segmentation and perhaps noun-phrase chunking baselines

The supervised contrastive objective is straightforward and likely stronger than triplet/regression losses in this setting. One possible issue: the formula shown seems to omit the positive from the denominator in the standard supervised contrastive form, or at least differs from the usual formulation. Please verify whether the equation is exactly what was implemented.

The adaptive expansion stage is intuitive, but I wonder whether averaging distances to all seeds is robust when seed sets are heterogeneous. Some attributes may have multimodal value distributions. Did the authors try centroid-based or nearest-neighbor-based assignment instead?

The self-supervised bullet-point heuristic is plausible, though noisy. It assumes spans in the same bullet point are semantically related and spans in different bullet points of the same product are less related. This may hold often, but not always. It would help to quantify how sensitive results are to this assumption, or compare with simpler document-level co-occurrence.

The latent-attribute module is interesting, but its contribution seems modest relative to the whole system. The paper says it contributes around 70% of the regularization gain, but the absolute gain from regularization is only about 2.2 partial F1 over Amacer-R. This is still useful, but the paper should calibrate claims accordingly.

Experiments

The baseline suite is decent, but there are some gaps:
- Why not compare against a noun-phrase extraction baseline for candidate generation?
- Why not compare against a simpler clustering pipeline using SBERT embeddings or instruction-tuned embeddings?
- Since the method uses BERT-Large for all models, it would be useful to know whether gains persist with stronger modern encoders.

The comparison to closed-world tagging models is somewhat unfair as an open-world benchmark, though still informative. The more relevant comparisons are OA-Mine and the syntax-based ablations.

I appreciated the OA-Mine* and Amacer* variants, which help separate segmentation from syntax-based candidates. Still, I would like one more ablation:
- Amacer with syntax candidates but without adaptive expansion, and with a stronger clustering alternative than DBSCAN
- Or adaptive expansion using raw BERT embeddings without contrastive learning

The statistical significance statement is too brief. Please specify:
- Number of runs
- What units were used for the t-test (categories? random seeds?)
- Variance across runs

Interpretation of results

The gains on new attributes are encouraging. However, “discovering values from 39% new types” is a bit vague. Does this mean at least one value from 39% of unseen gold types is recovered? If so, this is a fairly weak notion of type discovery. It would help to report:
- Number/proportion of unseen gold types with at least one correctly extracted value
- Average cluster purity for unseen-type clusters
- Whether discovered clusters correspond cleanly to coherent new attributes or are mixed

The qualitative examples are useful, especially Table 6 showing that unseen location-like attributes are often absorbed into existing clusters. This highlights that the system often extracts the spans but fails to create a genuinely new type. That is an important limitation and should be emphasized more.

Clarity and presentation

The paper is generally readable and well organized. The motivation and pipeline are easy to follow.

A few issues:
- There are several grammatical errors and awkward phrasings throughout. The paper would benefit from proofreading.
- Some notation is slightly inconsistent, e.g., h^p vs h_p.
- The loss equations should be checked carefully for correctness and consistency with implementation.
- The distinction between exact-match clustering evaluation and partial-match span evaluation could be explained more clearly.

Questions for the authors

1. How much of the final gain comes from candidate generation alone versus representation learning versus grouping?
2. What is inter-annotator agreement on the test set?
3. How many random seeds were used, and what is the variance?
4. Can you report candidate-span recall/precision before clustering?
5. How sensitive is the method to the number K of latent attributes?
6. How often does the model create genuinely new coherent clusters, rather than assigning unseen values to existing seed types?
7. Would the approach still work if product profiles were unavailable for deriving POS patterns?

Suggestions for improvement

1. Strengthen evaluation
Report more standard end-to-end extraction metrics and cluster-quality analyses, especially for unseen types. If pseudo-F1 is retained, justify it more carefully and supplement it with clearer metrics.

2. Better isolate contributions
Add experiments that quantify candidate generation quality directly and disentangle gains from syntax patterns versus embedding learning versus regularization.

3. Expand dataset analysis
Provide annotation agreement, more category-level breakdowns, and perhaps a transfer experiment where POS patterns learned from some categories are applied to another.

4. Improve baselines
Include simpler syntax baselines, noun-phrase extraction, and stronger embedding baselines.

5. Temper claims on new-type discovery
The method improves unseen-type handling, but the qualitative evidence suggests true new-type induction remains limited.

Recommendation

Weak Accept

Rationale

I lean positive because the paper tackles an important and underexplored setting, introduces a useful dataset, and shows convincing empirical improvements with a practical method. The work is not conceptually groundbreaking at the component level, and the evaluation methodology raises concerns, but the overall contribution is still meaningful for the community, especially as a benchmark/task formulation paper with a solid applied method. Strengthening the evaluation and clarifying the contribution of each component would make the paper significantly stronger.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting for e-commerce, where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover values of previously unseen attribute types without explicitly naming them. The authors create a new dataset, WoaM, spanning four Amazon product categories with seed attributes, raw product text, and human-annotated test data. They propose Amacer, a pipeline that generates candidate spans using POS-pattern-based syntax heuristics, learns span representations with supervised contrastive learning from seed attributes, and improves discovery of unseen attributes via two additional signals: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive objective and an unsupervised latent-attribute topic-model-like regularizer. Final grouping combines adaptive expansion for seed attributes with DBSCAN for remaining candidates. Experiments show substantial gains over prior weakly supervised/open-world baselines, especially on overall pseudo-F1 and on new attribute discovery.
strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and underexplored setting: open-world attribute mining with only light supervision, which is more realistic than closed-world tagging or zero-shot extraction requiring explicit target attribute names.
The task formulation is clear and meaningful: jointly expanding known attribute vocabularies and discovering entirely new attribute types.

The dataset contribution appears valuable, with human-annotated test data, multiple product categories, and inclusion of both titles and bullet points, which better reflects realistic e-commerce text.
The proposed pipeline is intuitive and modular, with sensible decomposition into candidate generation, representation learning, and clustering/grouping.
The syntax-based candidate generation is simple, scalable, and empirically stronger than segmentation-based alternatives in this setting.
The use of supervised contrastive learning for seed expansion is well motivated and cleaner than more cumbersome triplet/regression formulations.
The implicit-signal components for unseen attribute discovery are novel in this context, especially the latent-attribute regularization inspired by neural topic models.
Experimental results are fairly comprehensive, including multiple baselines, ablations, exact vs partial span matching, seed vs new attribute analysis, and title vs bullet-point breakdowns.
The paper includes useful qualitative analysis and candid discussion of limitations such as noisy candidates and topic collapse.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol relies on a nonstandard 'pseudo-F1' that averages clustering metrics into a pseudo-precision term before combining with recall; this is somewhat ad hoc and may make interpretation difficult.

The method is a multi-stage pipeline with several heuristics and hyperparameters (POS patterns, adaptive thresholds, DBSCAN settings, latent attribute count), making it harder to isolate which components are fundamentally responsible for gains.
Candidate generation depends heavily on POS tagging quality and handcrafted syntactic assumptions; this may limit robustness across domains, languages, or noisier product text.
The dataset covers only four product categories, so claims about general open-world applicability may be somewhat limited.

Although the paper emphasizes new attribute discovery, performance on new types remains substantially lower than on seed types, and qualitative examples show frequent confusion of new types with existing ones.

The latent attribute component is interesting but somewhat loosely connected to the final clustering objective; the paper does not fully clarify why the learned latent topics should align with attribute types rather than broader product concepts.

Some comparisons may not be entirely apples-to-apples because candidate generation differs substantially across systems, and improvements may partly stem from better span proposal rather than better open-world attribute modeling.
The paper does not provide much annotation-quality evidence for the human-labeled test set, such as inter-annotator agreement or adjudication details.
soundness_issues: The proposed methodology is generally reasonable, but the main evaluation metric is not standard and may obscure trade-offs between clustering purity and extraction coverage.

The adaptive expansion threshold is based on average intra-seed cosine distance scaled by a tuned factor; while intuitive, this heuristic lacks strong theoretical justification and may be sensitive to seed-set composition.

The self-supervised assumption that spans within the same bullet point are semantically related and spans across bullet points of the same product are negatives is noisy and may introduce false supervision.

The unsupervised latent-attribute model may capture topical/product-category structure rather than attribute-type structure; the paper acknowledges repetitive/collapsed latent attributes but does not deeply analyze their effect.
Because training supervision is obtained by string matching seed values in the corpus, there may be bias toward lexical overlap and undercoverage of paraphrastic attribute expressions.

The absence of reported annotation agreement for the test set weakens confidence in the gold standard, especially given the acknowledged subjectivity of span boundaries and attribute typing in open-world settings.
